# Vela: language, tests, and mocks

> Practical reference for AI assistants writing `.vela` source. Covers core
> syntax, common standard APIs, `sdk:test`, and `sdk:mock` with runnable examples.

Vela is a statically typed embedded scripting language for native C++ applications.
It is in active development. This guide describes current supported usage; detailed
contracts are linked from [llms.txt](llms.txt) and [the documentation index](docs/README.md).
Check the relevant topic before using an API not shown here. Application-specific
host functions must come from the application's declarations.

## A complete program

```vela
class Counter {
  value: int;
  step: int = 1;

  next(): int {
    this.value += this.step;
    return this.value;
  }
}

func main(): void {
  const counter = Counter(value: 40, step: 2);
  print('answer: ${counter.next()}'); // answer: 42
}
```

Statements use semicolons; blocks use braces. Top-level functions use `func`.
Methods omit `func`. Type annotations follow names: `name: Type`. Call constructors
as `Counter(...)` without `new`. `print(value)` writes one value and a newline.
Execution starts at `main`; an async main returns `Future<T>`. The CLI prints a
non-void main result and waits for a returned Future. Successful execution exits 0,
including when an integer main result is nonzero. Unhandled execution errors exit 1.

## Values, bindings, and numeric rules

| Spelling | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `int` | Signed 64-bit integer; integer arithmetic is checked |
| `double` | IEEE 754 binary64 floating-point value |
| `bool` | `true` or `false`; conditions require bool |
| `string` | Immutable validated UTF-8 text |
| `void` | No result; not a storable value |
| `T?` | T or null |
| `T[]` | Mutable, growable, invariant array of T |
| `dynamic` | Explicitly dynamic value; operations and typed conversions are checked |

Use `let` for rebinding and `const` for a fixed binding. Both allow local type
inference and require initializers. Const does not freeze an object or collection.
Locals are visible only after their initializer. Nested scopes may shadow outer
bindings. Function signatures and type declarations can refer to later declarations.

```vela
func main(): void {
  let count: int = 40;
  count += 2;
  const fraction: double = count.toDouble() / 2.0;
  const whole: int = 42.9.toInt();
  const hex: int = 0x2a;
  const binary: int = 0b101010;
  const octal: int = 0o52;
  print(fraction); // 21
  print(whole + hex + binary + octal); // 168
}
```

Int and double never mix implicitly in arithmetic, assignments, arguments, or
returns. Use `toInt()` / `toDouble()`; `as` is a type check, not a numeric conversion.
Double-to-int truncates toward zero and rejects non-finite or out-of-range values.
Write `1.0` for a double literal, `1` for int. Use `int.parse(text)` or
`int.tryParse(text)` for numeric text; tryParse returns null for invalid text.
No truthiness, `undefined`, `number`, `any`, union types, or general rest/spread
syntax is provided. Integer literals support decimal, hex, binary, and octal;
digit separators and numeric suffixes are unsupported.

## Functions, lambdas, and generics

```vela
type IntOperation = (int) => int;

func add(left: int, right: int = 2): int {
  return left + right;
}

func apply(value: int, operation: IntOperation): int {
  return operation(value);
}

func identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}

func main(): void {
  const twice: IntOperation = value => value * 2;
  const increment = (value: int) => value + 1;
  print(add(right: 2, left: 40)); // 42
  print(apply(21, twice)); // 42
  print(increment(identity(41))); // 42
}
```

Function declarations require parameter and return types. Function type annotations
contain types only, such as `(int, int) => int`; calls through function values use
positional arguments. Lambdas use `=>` with an expression or block body. Context can
supply lambda parameter types; otherwise annotate them. A block lambda with an
explicit result uses `(value: int): int => { return value + 1; }`.

Ordinary declared calls support named arguments. Supplied arguments evaluate in
source order, followed by omitted defaults in parameter order. Null is a value
and does not request a default. Captured mutable bindings are shared by closures;
bound method values retain their receiver.

Functions, classes, interfaces, aliases, and methods can declare type parameters.
Use `T extends SomeInterface` for a bound. Type arguments can be inferred at calls
when constraints establish them; use explicit `<...>` otherwise. Type annotations
remain complete. Aliases are transparent, not new nominal types. Containers such
as `T[]`, `Map<K, V>`, and `Set<T>` are invariant. See
[generics](docs/en/generics.md) and [inference](docs/en/type_inference.md).

## Nullability and checked dynamic values

```vela
func describe(name: string?): string {
  if (name == null) { return 'anonymous'; }
  return name.toUpperCase();
}

func main(): void {
  const name: string? = null;
  print(describe(name)); // anonymous
  print(name?.length ?? 0); // 0
  const values: int[]? = null;
  print(values?.[0] ?? 42); // 42: index access is skipped
  const mixed: dynamic[] = [42, 'Vela'];
  const answer = mixed[0] as int;
  print(answer); // 42
}
```

`T?` allows null; it does not make a field constructor argument optional. Use an
initializer/default when omission is intended. A bare null initializer needs an
explicit nullable type. `int?[]` is an array of nullable ints; `int[]?` is a nullable
array of ints. An existing `int[]` cannot become `int?[]` by assignment.

Null checks refine stable locals and parameters. Fields and indexed elements are
not promoted; copy them into a local before checking. `?.` and `?.[index]` skip
access and argument/index evaluation for null receivers. `??` evaluates its right
operand only when the left is null. `??=` and postfix non-null assertions are
unsupported. Use `is Type` for a checked type test and `as Type` for a checked cast.
Dynamic retains the actual value type and does not permit numeric coercion or
arbitrary object properties. Prefer explicit casts or `is` refinement at dynamic
boundaries; implicit dynamic-to-concrete conversions produce warnings.

## Control flow, enums, and matching

```vela
enum Mode { off, on }

func label(mode: Mode): string {
  return match (mode) {
    Mode.off => 'off',
    Mode.on => 'on',
  };
}

func main(): void {
  let total = 0;
  for (let index = 0; index < 3; index++) {
    if (index == 1) { continue; }
    total += index;
  }
  for (const value in [20, 22]) { total += value; }
  while (total < 45) { total++; }
  switch (total) {
    case 45:
      print(label(Mode.on)); // on
      break;
    default:
      print('unexpected');
  }
  print(total > 0 ? 'positive' : 'zero'); // positive
}
```

Use `if`, `else`, `while`, C-style `for`, collection `for (const value in collection)`,
`break`, `continue`, `switch`, and `return`. Collection loops bind one read-only
name; arrays and Sets yield values, Maps yield a snapshot of keys. No `for...of`
or loop destructuring exists. Enum members must be qualified as `Mode.on`.

Switch selectors use non-null int, bool, string, or enum types. Labels must be
same-type constants. Empty labels can share a body; a non-empty branch must exit
before a following label. Match is an exhaustive expression: arms use `=>`, `_`
is a wildcard, and `let value` binds the selected value. Nullable matches can use
`null => ...` followed by `let value => ...`. Pattern guards and destructuring
are unsupported. Non-void functions must return on every finite path.

Operators include arithmetic, comparisons, `==` / `!=`, `&&` / `||` / `!`, bitwise
operators, shifts including `>>>`, compound assignments, prefix/postfix `++` / `--`,
and conditional `condition ? left : right`. Equality uses `==`, not `===`.

## Classes and interfaces

```vela
interface Measurable {
  measure(): int;
}

class Counter implements Measurable {
  private current: int = 0;

  constructor(initial: int) {
    this.current = initial;
  }

  get value(): int { return this.current; }
  set value(next: int): void { this.current = next; }
  measure(): int { return this.current; }
}

class BonusCounter extends Counter {
  constructor(initial: int) { super(initial); }
  override measure(): int { return super.measure() + 2; }
}

func main(): void {
  const counter = BonusCounter(40);
  const measured: Measurable = counter;
  print(measured.measure()); // 42
  counter.value = 41;
  print(counter.value); // 41
}
```

Members are public by default; use `private` for private members and `static` for
class members. Access fields with `this.field` inside methods. Interfaces use
method signatures and require explicit `implements`; matching shape alone does
not implement an interface. Classes support single inheritance and multiple
implemented interfaces. Overrides use `override`; `super.method()` calls the base
implementation. Interface inheritance and interface properties are unsupported.

Without an explicit constructor parameter list, public instance fields become named
constructor parameters. Fields without initializers are required; initialized fields
supply defaults. Private/static fields do not become constructor parameters.
`constructor { ... }` adds a body after generated field initialization.
`constructor(...) { ... }` instead defines the complete parameter list and must
initialize required fields. `constructor()` explicitly declares zero parameters.
See [construction and inheritance](docs/en/core_language.md).

## Strings and collections

```vela
func main(): void {
  const values: int[] = [];
  values.push(20, 22);
  const total = values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0);
  const labels = values.map(value => value.toString());
  print(labels.join(', ')); // 20, 22

  const scores: Map<string, int> = {'Vela': total};
  scores.set('other', 7);
  for (const key in scores) { print('${key}: ${scores.get(key) ?? 0}'); }

  const names = Set<string>();
  names.add('Vela');
  print(names.has('Vela')); // true

  const text = 'A中😀';
  print(text.length); // 3 code points
  print(text.byteLength); // 8 bytes
  const builder = String();
  builder.append('Hello, ');
  builder.append('Vela');
  print(builder.toString()); // Hello, Vela
}
```

Both single and double quotes support `${expression}` interpolation; backticks are
not string delimiters. Interpolation accepts primitive/null values, not arbitrary
objects or arrays. Strings index and slice by Unicode code point. Use `byteLength`
for UTF-8 bytes and grapheme APIs for user-perceived characters. Lowercase `string`
is immutable text; capitalized `String` is a mutable builder.

| Type | Common API |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | `length`, `byteLength`, indexing, `slice(start, end)`, `includes(text)`, `indexOf(text)`, `startsWith(prefix)`, `endsWith(suffix)`, `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()` |
| `T[]` | `length`, `capacity`, `push(...)`, `pop()`, `shift()`, `unshift(...)`, `splice(...)`, `slice()`, `clear()`, `reserve(n)`, `join(separator)` |
| Array algorithms | `map`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `findIndex`, `reduce(callback, initialValue)`, `sort(compare)` |
| `Set<T>` | `size`, `add(value)`, `has(value)`, `delete(value)`, `clear()`, `values()`, `union`, `intersection`, `difference` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `size`, `set(key, value)`, `get(key)`, `has(key)`, `delete(key)`, `clear()`, `keys()`, `values()` |

Array pop/shift and Map get return nullable results. Reduce requires an initial
value. Empty array literals need an element type from context. Arrays have read-only
length; assigning an out-of-bounds element does not grow them. Set/Map use `.size`.
Collection snapshots preserve insertion order; Map/Set language equality compares
identity, while test `equals` performs deep collection matching.

Map literals use `{keyExpression: valueExpression}`. Quote string keys: `{'name': 42}`;
`{name: 42}` reads a variable named name. Empty `{}` needs a Map type context.
Mixed values need an explicit dynamic value context. A Map-returning expression
lambda needs parentheses: `value => ({'answer': value})`. Object/Set literals,
field shorthand, destructuring, and collection spread are unsupported.

## Modules and standard globals

```vela
// File: lib/math.vela
export func triple(value: int): int { return value * 3; }
```

```vela
// File: module_main.vela
import 'lib/math' as math;

func main(): void {
  print(math.triple(14)); // 42
  print(Math.sqrt(9.0)); // 3
}
```

Each file has its own top-level scope. Export declarations explicitly. Use
`import 'relative/path';` to import exports directly or `as prefix` for qualified
names. Relative paths resolve from the importing file; extensionless imports select
`.vela` directly, with no index-file probing. Imports are not implicit re-exports.
No JavaScript named-import braces or namespace declaration blocks exist.

Math, Random, performance, Date, DateParts, JSON, and Error are default globals.
Common operations are `Math.sqrt(9.0)`, `Math.random()`, `Random.nextInt(10)`,
`performance.now()` (double monotonic milliseconds), and `Date.now()` (int Unix
milliseconds). Math numeric inputs use double. Do not add `std:` imports.
Testing and mocking require explicit `sdk:test` and `sdk:mock` imports.

`JSON.parse(text)` returns dynamic: objects are `Map<string, dynamic>`, arrays are
`dynamic[]`. Read object keys with `.get('key')`, not invented field access.
`JSON.stringify(value)` encodes supported values. `JSON.parse<T>(text)` and
`JSON.safeParse<T>(text)` require explicit target types; the latter returns a
result whose `success` selects `value` or `error`. See [typed JSON](docs/en/typed_json.md).
RegExp, ByteArray, ByteData, reflection, date conversion, and other specialized
APIs have dedicated contracts linked from [llms.txt](llms.txt).

## Exceptions and asynchronous work

```vela
async func load(value: int): Future<int> {
  await sleep(1);
  if (value < 0) { throw Error(message: 'negative value'); }
  return value;
}

async func main(): Future<void> {
  const values = await Future.wait([load(20), load(22)]);
  print(values[0] + values[1]); // 42
  try {
    await load(-1);
  } catch (error: Error) {
    print(error.message); // negative value
  } finally {
    print('finished');
  }
}
```

Throw a non-null class/interface object, not a string or number. Error is a default
class; custom throwable classes need no Error base. Use `catch (name: Type)`, a
final `catch (name: dynamic)`, or a binding-free `catch { ... }`. Finally runs on
ordinary control-flow exit and exception unwinding.

Async functions and lambdas return `Future<T>` and use `await` inside async bodies.
Async lambdas use `async (): Future<void> => { ... }`. Calls execute synchronously
until return, error, or await; async does not create a thread. Use Future, not
Promise. APIs include `Future.value`, `Future.wait`, `Future.microtask`,
`Completer<T>()`, `sleep(milliseconds)`, and `Timer.after(milliseconds, callback)`.
Await propagates failed Futures through ordinary catch/finally. Program entry
completion stops background tasks; await work required by the program's result.
See [async contracts](docs/en/async_tasks.md) before adding composition or timers.

## Test project and commands

Tests use the embedded `sdk:test` source library. The Vela runner executes tests;
`python -m tools.vl test` tests the compiler's C++ implementation instead.
Create a strict JSON `vela.json` at the application project root:

```json
{
  "test": {
    "paths": ["tests"],
    "filename": "*_test.vela",
    "timeout": "30s",
    "concurrency": 2,
    "tags": {"unit": {}}
  }
}
```

```text
vela test
vela test tests/language_test.vela
vela test --plain-name "arithmetic"
vela test --tags "unit && !slow"
vela test --reporter json
vela test --list
```

The runner finds the nearest vela.json upwards from the working directory, or uses
`--config FILE`. A `test` object is required. Without CLI paths, test.paths must
be explicit and nonempty; there is no implicit test directory. CLI paths replace
configured paths. Config paths are relative to the config; CLI paths to the current
directory. Directly selected files need not match the filename glob. Config rejects
comments, trailing commas, duplicate keys, and unknown fields.

Each suite has an independent Isolate and module state. Tests within a suite run
sequentially; concurrency is between suites. `--list` executes registration but no
test bodies or hooks. JSON reporting is newline-delimited events, not one JSON
array; use the final `done` event for final counts. No selected tests is a failure;
all selected tests explicitly skipped is success.

## Test registration, lifecycle, and assertions

```vela
// File: tests/language_test.vela
import 'sdk:test';

func main(): void {
  group('arithmetic', () => {
    let values: int[] = [];
    setUp(() => { values = [20, 22]; });
    tearDown(() => { values.clear(); });

    test('sum', () => {
      expect(values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0), equals(42));
      expect(values, hasLength(2));
    });

    test('Future result', async (): Future<void> => {
      await expectLater(Future.value(42), completion(equals(42)));
    });

    test('callback', () => {
      const done = expectAsync1<int>((value: int): void => {
        expect(value, equals(42));
      });
      done(42);
    });

    test('original exception', () => {
      const problem = Error(message: 'invalid');
      expect((): void => { throw problem; }, throwsA(same(problem)));
    });
  }, tags: ['unit']);
}
```

Main registers the test tree. Group bodies run synchronously and must return void.
Use the same `test(description, body)` for sync and async tests; there is no
`testAsync`. A test or lifecycle callback must be callable with zero arguments.
Ordinary return values are ignored; returned Futures are awaited. Registration
APIs take dynamic callbacks, so annotate lambda parameters when context is absent.

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `test(description, body, ...)` | Register a test |
| `group(description, body, ...)` | Register a nested group synchronously |
| `setUp(callback)`, `tearDown(callback)` | Before/after each test in scope |
| `setUpAll(callback)`, `tearDownAll(callback)` | Once before/after selected group tests |
| `addTearDown(callback)` | Dynamic cleanup in the active test/setup scope |
| `expect(actual, matcher, reason: ...)` | Synchronous check or tracked async expectation |
| `expectLater(actual, matcher, reason: ...)` | Tracked expectation returning Future<void> |
| `fail(message)` | Throw TestFailure |
| `expectAsync0(callback, count: ..., max: ...)` | Track a zero-argument callback |
| `expectAsync1<T>(callback, count: ..., max: ...)` | Track a one-argument callback; specify T |

Test/group metadata accepts `skip: true` or a reason string, `tags: 'unit'` or an
array of strings, and `timeout: Timeout(milliseconds: 1000)`, `Timeout.factor(2.0)`,
or `Timeout.none()`. Timeout is an inactivity limit, not preemptive interruption
of synchronous code or a host call.

Setups run outer to inner in registration order. Dynamic cleanup runs last-in-first-out,
then teardowns run inner to outer in reverse registration order. Callbacks and their
Futures are awaited sequentially. Cleanup still runs after a test failure.
`addTearDown` in setUpAll belongs to the group; otherwise it belongs to the active
test. Async expectations remain attached to their originating test even when the
caller omits await. Prefer await when subsequent code depends on their completion.

| Matcher | Usage |
| --- | --- |
| `equals(value)` | Deep equality for arrays, Maps, and Sets; ordinary objects retain identity semantics |
| `same(value)` | Identity comparison |
| `isNull`, `isNotNull`, `isTrue`, `isFalse`, `isEmpty`, `isNotEmpty` | Matcher constants, with no parentheses |
| `greaterThan(value)`, `lessThan(value)` | Same-kind numeric comparisons |
| `closeTo(3.0, 0.01)` | Double tolerance; no int/double coercion |
| `contains(value)`, `hasLength(n)` | String/collection matching |
| `orderedEquals(values)`, `unorderedEquals(values)` | Ordered or one-to-one unordered matching |
| `isNot(matcher)`, `allOf([a, b])`, `anyOf([a, b])` | Composition; allOf/anyOf take arrays |
| `predicate(callback, description)` | `(dynamic) => bool` predicate |
| `throwsA(matcher)` | A zero-argument function throwing, or a Future failing, with the matched original object |
| `completes`, `completion(matcher)` | Successful Future completion, optionally matching its result |

Passing a plain expected value to expect wraps it as equals. Test equals does not
change the language's `==` semantics. Custom synchronous matchers implement
`Matcher.match(actual: dynamic): MatchResult`; async matchers implement
`AsyncMatcher.matchAsync(actual: dynamic): Future<MatchResult>`.
Exact declarations are in [the test SDK](compiler/sdk/test.vela).

## Generate and use interface mocks

Define dependencies as exported interfaces and generate ordinary Vela source:

```vela
// File: lib/user_repository.vela
export interface UserRepository {
  load(id: int): Future<string>;
  save(id: int, name: string): void;
}
```

```text
vela mock lib/user_repository.vela --interface UserRepository -o tests/user_repository.mocks.vela
vela mock lib/user_repository.vela --interface UserRepository -o tests/user_repository.mocks.vela --check
```

Generation is explicit; compilation, testing, and LSP do not regenerate files.
Run `--check` in CI to detect a missing or stale generated module. Select at least
one exported interface with `--interface`; repeat the option for multiple interfaces.

```vela
// File: tests/repository_test.vela
import 'sdk:test';
import 'sdk:mock' as mock;
import '../lib/user_repository' as api;
import './user_repository.mocks.vela' as generated;

async func refresh(repository: api.UserRepository, id: int): Future<string> {
  const name = await repository.load(id);
  repository.save(id: id, name: name);
  return name;
}

func main(): void {
  test('loads and saves a user', async (): Future<void> => {
    const session = mock.MockSession();
    const repository = generated.MockUserRepository(session: session);

    mock.when(repository.calls.load(42)).thenAnswer(
      async (invocation: mock.MockInvocation): Future<string> => {
        expect(invocation.argument('id'), equals(42));
        return 'Alice';
      }
    );
    mock.when(repository.calls.save(42, 'Alice')).thenDo(
      (invocation: mock.MockInvocation): void => {
        expect(invocation.argumentAt(1), equals('Alice'));
      }
    );

    expect(await refresh(repository.object, 42), equals('Alice'));
    mock.verifyInOrder([
      repository.calls.load(42),
      repository.calls.save(42, 'Alice'),
    ]);
    mock.verifyNoMoreInteractions(repository.control);
  });
}
```

The generated wrapper exposes `.object` with the real interface type, `.calls`
for call patterns, and `.control` for history management. Constructing a pattern
does not execute or record a business call. Configure with
`mock.when(repository.calls.load(...))`, not a real `.object.load(...)` call or a
Mockito-style recording closure.

Create MockSession in a test or its setUp, never in registration or setUpAll for
sharing across tests. It belongs to that test and closes automatically after all
its cleanup callbacks. Explicit `session.close()` closes it early. Calls,
configuration, and verification cannot cross test scopes. One session can hold
multiple mocks for cross-mock ordering.

The generator supports exported non-generic interfaces with ordinary methods,
including concrete generic types, nullable values, function types, void, and
Future results. Open generic interfaces and generic methods are unsupported.
Classes, constructors, static methods, top-level functions, and builtins cannot
be patched at runtime; inject interfaces or function values instead.

## Stub responses and argument matching

| Response | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `thenReturn(value)` | Fixed non-Future, non-void result; reused on every matching call |
| `thenReturnInOrder(values)` | Nonempty finite sequence; exhaustion fails |
| `thenThrow(error)` | Synchronously throw the original throwable object |
| `thenAnswer(callback)` | One MockInvocation argument; return the declared value/Future |
| `thenDo(callback)` | Void method only; one MockInvocation argument, synchronous void result |

Every real call requires a stub, including void calls. Missing stubs fail with
MockMissingStub. Complete every when builder with one response. The last configured
matching stub wins. Exhausting a sequence fails rather than selecting an older stub.
For Future methods, use thenAnswer to create the Future in the actual call context;
thenReturn does not accept Futures. ThenThrow still throws synchronously for a Future
method; return a failed Future from thenAnswer when asynchronous failure is intended.

Patterns accept ordinary values (deep equals), synchronous sdk:test matchers, or
`mock.any` (including null). Named and positional call forms normalize to the same
declared parameter order. Use `same(value)` for reference identity. Capture patterns
`mock.captureAny` and `mock.captureThat(matcher)` are only valid for verification,
not stubbing or untilCalled. Async matchers are unsupported for arguments.

MockInvocation provides `argumentAt(index)`, `argument(name)`, `arguments`,
`sequence`, `methodName`, and source/identity metadata. Argument arrays are shallow
copies; object arguments remain shared references. Later mutation can affect later
deep matching. Extract a snapshot explicitly in a response when needed.

## Function mocks, capture, and asynchronous observation

```vela
// File: tests/function_mock_test.vela
import 'sdk:test';
import 'sdk:mock' as mock;

func apply(value: int, operation: (int) => int): int {
  return operation(value);
}

func main(): void {
  test('function dependency and capture', () => {
    const function = mock.MockFunction1<int, int>(mock.MockSession());
    mock.when(function.query(mock.any)).thenReturn(42);
    expect(apply(7, function.function), equals(42));
    const result = mock.verify(function.query(mock.captureAny)).called(1);
    expect(result.captured, equals([7]));
    mock.verifyNoMoreInteractions(function.control);
  });

  test('observe a call', async (): Future<void> => {
    const function = mock.MockFunction0<int>(mock.MockSession());
    mock.when(function.query()).thenReturn(42);
    const observed = mock.untilCalled(function.query());
    expect(function.function(), equals(42));
    const invocation = await observed;
    expect(invocation.arguments, isEmpty);
    mock.verify(function.query()).called(1);
    mock.verifyNoMoreInteractions(function.control);
  });
}
```

Use MockFunction0<R>, MockFunction1<A, R>, or MockFunction2<A, B, R> for typed
function dependencies; `.function` is the callable, `.query(...)` creates patterns,
and `.control` manages history. Supply type arguments explicitly or through a
complete contextual type. R cannot be void. Void equivalents are MockVoidFunction0,
MockVoidFunction1<A>, and MockVoidFunction2<A, B>; configure them with thenDo.
Use a generated interface for larger function signatures.

| Verification API | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `mock.verify(call).called(n)` | Exactly n unverified calls; n may also be a count Matcher |
| `mock.verifyNever(call)` | Zero matching unverified calls |
| `mock.verifyInOrder([call1, call2])` | Ordered distinct unverified calls in one session |
| `mock.verifyZeroInteractions(control)` | No history at all, including verified calls |
| `mock.verifyNoMoreInteractions(control)` | No remaining unverified calls |
| `mock.clearInteractions(control)` | Clear history, keep stubs and sequence position |
| `mock.reset(control)` | Clear history/stubs and invalidate pending operations for that mock |
| `mock.untilCalled(call)` | Future<MockInvocation> for earliest matching history or the next matching call |

Successful verification consumes matching records; failure consumes nothing.
Called(0) consumes nothing. In-order verification commits only if the complete
sequence succeeds; unrelated intermediate calls remain unverified. Captures are
published only on successful verification, flattened by call order then parameter
order. Do not verify the same consumed calls again with a different operation.

UntilCalled also sees verified history and does not consume calls. It completes
when the invocation is recorded, not when its response or Future finishes. Await
the method result separately when completion matters. It is tracked by the test
even if not awaited. Reset fails pending waits with MockReset; close fails them
with MockSessionClosed. Clearing history leaves future-call waits registered.
Usage, missing-stub, exhausted-sequence, and verification errors use the test
failure channel. See [mock contracts](docs/zh-CN/testing.md#12-mock-扩展) and
[SDK declarations](compiler/sdk/mock.vela) for exact behavior.

## Validate generated Vela code

```text
vela check app.vela
vela run app.vela
vela check tests/repository_test.vela
vela test --config vela.json
vela fmt --check .
```

Use the installed vela executable, or the repository build at
`out/debug/vela.exe` / `out/release/vela.exe` on Windows. Check source and imports,
run programs with known outputs, generate/check mocks before their tests, and run
the Vela test runner. Syntax/type checking alone does not execute tests or validate
stub responses. Production AOT rejects sdk:test and sdk:mock imports; keep them in
development/test modules.

Before completing generated code, check the recurring mistakes: use func, postfix
types, explicit numeric conversion, ClassName(...) construction, qualified enum
members, collection for-in, Future<T>, explicit SDK imports, synchronous groups,
per-test mock sessions, `.calls` patterns, and explicit void stubs. Consult the
current contract instead of inventing missing APIs from another language.
